prompt: Why is a model call the hardest case for the rule that request bodies stay out of logs?

choices.text: Model providers require every prompt to be logged by the client
choices.why: No provider requires that; it is a decision of whoever runs the application.

choices.text: Prompts are too large to fit in an ordinary log line
choices.why: Size is not the issue; what they carry is.

choices.text: OpenTelemetry cannot record a request body unless it is a span
choices.why: It can record text in logs and spans alike.

choices.text: The body is what is being observed
choices.why: Right. Without the question, a trace cannot explain a wrong answer.

prompt: Match each job to how long it needs the text.
right_distractors: for as long as the account exists

prompt: A team redacts the customer's message before the prompt is built, and records the model's reply as it comes. What can still leak?

choices.text: Nothing, since the input was clean
choices.why: The retrieved sources and the reply were never cleaned.

choices.text: The API key, which the reply echoes
choices.why: A key is not in what the model reads, so it cannot repeat it.

choices.text: What the retrieved sources carry, through the reply
choices.why: Right. The prompt carries more than the customer wrote, and the reply can repeat any of it.

choices.text: The span's trace id
choices.why: A trace id is not personal data; it identifies a request.

prompt: How many of the week's 56 order requests carried something redact() would remove?
The scan found nothing to redact in help requests and something in every order request. What does that suggest for a retention policy?

choices.text: Decide per feature: the risk is concentrated
choices.why: Right. Personal data concentrates where a feature is about a particular person.

choices.text: Treat every trace the same, since the average is low
choices.why: The average hides that one feature is almost all of the risk.

choices.text: Stop recording the help feature, which has nothing worth keeping
choices.why: Its text is what lets a wrong answer be debugged, and it carries no personal data.

choices.text: Redact only the summary feature, used by staff
choices.why: The order feature carried personal data in every request too.

prompt: What did scan.py not count, although it is in the order messages?

choices.text: E-mail addresses
choices.why: It counted 107.

choices.text: Names
choices.why: Right. A name has no shape for a pattern to find.

choices.text: Order numbers
choices.why: It counted 341.

choices.text: Telephone numbers written with a country code
choices.why: It counted 110 of those.

prompt: Why does a placeholder such as [email] beat a row of asterisks?

choices.text: It is shorter, so the span stays small
choices.why: Length is not the point; what it keeps is.

choices.text: It is reversible by whoever holds the key
choices.why: Nothing in [email] can be reversed; the address is gone.

choices.text: It keeps the fact that an address was given
choices.why: Right. The sentence stays readable and the fact survives without the value.

choices.text: Tracing tools reject asterisks in attributes
choices.why: They accept any string.

prompt: What is a canary, in a test of redaction?

choices.text: A real customer's message kept to check the patterns against
choices.why: That would keep exactly what the test exists to protect.

choices.text: The first span of each trace
choices.why: That is the root, not a canary.

choices.text: A pattern that matches everything
choices.why: That would remove every attribute and test nothing.

choices.text: A value sent on purpose that must never appear in the exported spans
choices.why: Right. Its absence is the evidence that redaction is on.

prompt: A team decides to store spans as they are and clean them nightly in the backend. Which problem does that NOT have?

choices.text: Copies made before the cleaning keep the original
choices.why: It has this one: queues, buffers and backups taken before the night.

choices.text: The traces cannot be searched by trace id
choices.why: Right, that one is fine: the trace id is untouched either way. The other three are real.

choices.text: The backend does not know about next month's new attribute
choices.why: It has this one too.

choices.text: A person asking what is held is owed the uncleaned copies too
choices.why: It has this one as well.

prompt: Where does leak.py put its second net?

choices.text: In a wrapper around the exporter
choices.why: Right. Every span passes there, whoever made it.

choices.text: In the prompt, before the call
choices.why: That is the first net, and it only covers what the assistant writes.

choices.text: In the tracing backend
choices.why: By then the original has already left the process.

choices.text: In the OpenAI SDK
choices.why: The SDK is untouched; OpenInference instruments it and the wrapper sits after.

prompt: Why does the wrapper build a new span instead of editing the attributes of the one it receives?

choices.text: Editing would change the trace id of every span it touched
choices.why: Attributes and ids are separate; the copy keeps the ids as they are.

choices.text: New spans are faster to export than old ones
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: OpenInference locks the spans it writes so no one else can read them
choices.why: Nothing is locked; any exporter receives them.

choices.text: A finished span is read-only in the Python SDK
choices.why: Right. So the exporter hands on a clean copy.

choices.why: It scored 0.85, well above 0.5.

choices.text: It labelled it a date, so the removal was luck
choices.why: Right. A different format of order number may not look like a date.

choices.text: Presidio removes every number it sees, whatever it is
choices.why: It left the expiry date at 0.5, and the ISBN.

choices.text: It removed it only in the second run
choices.why: It removed it in both runs.

prompt: Raising Presidio's threshold from 0 to 0.5 kept the ISBN. What else did it change?

choices.text: The telephone number, scored 0.40, now leaks
choices.why: Right. There is no threshold that removes everything personal and nothing else.

choices.text: Nothing else; the threshold only affects ISBNs
choices.why: It applies to every finding, whatever its type.

choices.text: The names stopped being found
choices.why: They scored 0.85 and were still found.

choices.text: The e-mail address stopped being found
choices.why: It scored 1.00.

prompt: Finding names in free text takes named-entity ___, which Presidio does with a spaCy model.
Why could the unkeyed hash of u021 be reversed in under a millisecond?

choices.text: SHA-256 is broken
choices.why: It is not; nothing about the hash was attacked.

choices.text: Sixteen characters is too short
choices.why: Even the full hash falls the same way; length is not the problem.

choices.text: The ids follow a known shape, so every guess is hashed and compared
choices.why: Right. Hashing a guessable value only adds a step.

choices.text: The key was printed
choices.why: There was no key: that was the point of the first line.

prompt: In the LGPD's terms, what is the keyed pseudonym in user.hash?

choices.text: Anonymised data, outside the law
choices.why: Whoever holds the key can reverse it, so it is not anonymous.

choices.text: Pseudonymised data, still personal
choices.why: Right. The trace store has to be treated accordingly.

choices.text: Sensitive personal data, like health or religion
choices.why: Nothing in a user id says anything of that kind.

choices.text: A credential, like a password or a token
choices.why: It grants no access to anything.

prompt: The pseudonym key is rotated every month. What still works?

choices.text: Following one person across a year of traces
choices.why: Each month's pseudonyms no longer join with the next month's.

choices.text: Reading the user id back from the trace without the key
choices.why: That never worked, with or without rotation.

choices.text: Counting per user within a month
choices.why: Right. Within one key, the same person gets the same value.

choices.text: Erasing a person's text after the key for that month is thrown away
choices.why: Without the key nobody can find which spans are theirs; the link is gone instead.

prompt: With PSEUDONYM_KEY empty, the assistant raised an error. Why is that better than an unkeyed fallback?

choices.text: A fallback would write reversible ids onto every span, silently
choices.why: Right. It would pass every test that does not look at the values.

choices.text: Errors are cheaper than hashes
choices.why: Cost has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: The SDK requires every attribute to be set
choices.why: A missing attribute is allowed.

choices.text: The customer would see the hash
choices.why: The hash is only on the span.

prompt: After expire.py ran with one day of life, how many root spans still carried a question?
A customer asks the shop to erase what it holds about them, and the text expires in five days. What should happen?

choices.text: Nothing; expiry will take care of it in five days
choices.why: The request is owed now, not when the schedule gets there.

choices.text: Every span in the store is deleted
choices.why: That destroys everybody's counts for one request.

choices.text: The key is rotated
choices.why: Rotation cuts future links; it does not delete what is already stored.

choices.text: Their text is deleted now, found by their pseudonym
choices.why: Right. Hash their id with the key and delete the text on those spans; the counts stay.
